# Module 2: Centering & Between/Within Effects {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Three Questions This Module Answers

- **What does my predictor's coefficient actually mean?** A customer's monthly disclosure engagement score carries two signals at once: customers who are generally more engaged (between-household) tend to save more, and in months when a household engages more than usual (within-household) their savings also increase. The standard random-intercept model conflates these into a single number that answers neither question cleanly.
- **When does a pooled estimate mislead?** The classic case: more promotional messages are sent to lower-tier consumer segments, and within each segment, more messages correlate with higher purchase intent. The aggregate relationship (more messages → lower intent) is real but backwards from the within-segment truth. This is Simpson's Paradox — a systematic feature of nested data, not a statistical curiosity.
- **How do I estimate both effects in one model?** Cluster-mean centering (CMC) separates the within-unit deviation from the unit mean. The Mundlak device includes both in a single regression. The Wald test tells you whether the within and between effects are statistically distinguishable — and therefore whether a pooled estimate is defensible.
:::

## The Subtlest Assumption

You have built a mixed-effects model, checked your residuals, verified convergence, and are ready to interpret your coefficients. There is one more question you need to answer before you do:

**What does your predictor's value actually mean?**

This sounds almost philosophical, but it has concrete, testable consequences. A predictor like "monthly financial disclosure engagement" can mean two different things in a household longitudinal dataset:

1. **Between-household effect:** Households that engage more with disclosures on average also tend to have higher savings rates (perhaps because financially motivated households both seek out disclosures and save more independently)
2. **Within-household effect:** In months when *this specific household* engages more than *their own average*, their savings rate increases

These two effects are not the same. They can point in opposite directions. They answer different scientific questions. And the standard random-intercept model, without careful centering, conflates them.

**Module 2 is about learning to see the difference — and to model it explicitly.**

## What This Module Covers

**Part 1: Centering Your Variables** introduces grand-mean centering (GMC) and cluster-mean centering (CMC), explains what each does to the interpretation of your coefficients, and provides a decision framework.

**Part 2: Between-Unit vs. Within-Unit Effects** shows how to simultaneously estimate both effects in a single model — the "Mundlak device" — and when the between and within effects diverge.

**Part 3: Simpson's Paradox** uses vivid examples to show how the relationship at the aggregate level can be completely opposite to the relationship at the individual level. This is not a statistical curiosity — it is a systematic feature of nested data that researchers frequently misinterpret.

## The Core Insight

Standard regression assumes your predictor has one meaning. In nested data, it has (at least) two: a within-unit meaning and a between-unit meaning. Centering is the tool that separates them.

> *"What does this coefficient represent — a within-household comparison or a between-household comparison?"* — asking this question before interpreting every coefficient will prevent some of the most consequential errors in applied multilevel research.
